title: Training around Perez, Piron and Moret; bass tone
summary: Learning among the old masters, Jimmy Johnson's bass tone, Blanton and the importance of round tone.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: No, but we were almost like relatives. I'd be at his house all the time. Yeah.
He went to... Old man George didn't have too much time for teaching.
Well, I imagine he was busy with his band.

Always busy. Always busy. And I had one of the musicians in my band as a product of those old bands, one of my first bands, that was old Jimmy Johnson. See, Jimmy played with Buddy Bowling and those guys.
Did he read much or was he fake?
No, he could read. No. But here's another case of a gifted musician. Even his tonation on the bass. It sounds strange to say a man gets a different tone out of a bass but that's certain.

You take like Blanton that was with Duke that died so young, well Blanton could make his bass sound like a shallow. And those are the things that a lot of musicians don't know how to get tonations out of their horns. You know the smart playing. It's not what we call a pinch tone, it's a round tone, it's big. And a lot of musicians in those days, the first thing they did, they studied their tonations. Like Big Al Loy, Lil Nelson, beautiful tone. Piku, tonation. Or listen to Bonnie's tone.
